title: Active voice
summary: Writing sentences so the person or organisation doing the action is the grammatical subject ("The team will send the report"), rather than the thing acted on ("The report will be sent"), so readers can see who does what.
selfCheck: Can the reader tell, sentence by sentence, who is responsible for each action?
Where I kept a passive, is the actor unknown, unimportant or obvious, or am I hiding who decided?
Did I mislabel any sentence as passive just because it uses "was" or describes the past?
steps: Find each sentence that has a form of "to be" plus a past participle (was sent, will be reviewed, has been approved).
Ask who does the action; if the sentence does not say, decide who should, and name them.
Rewrite with that actor as the subject and a strong verb right after it ("Finance will review the budget").
Address the reader as "you" when they are the one who must act.
Keep a passive only when the actor is unknown, unimportant or obvious, or when the thing acted on is what the paragraph is about.

example.situation: A project manager tells a client team what happens before go-live.
example.before: The test results will be reviewed and any outstanding issues must be resolved before the release can be approved.
example.after: Our QA lead will review the test results by Tuesday. Your team needs to fix any open issues by Thursday, and then I will approve the release.
example.why: The original names no one, so each side can assume the other owns the work; the rewrite assigns every action to a person and a date.

title: Aristotle's Rhetoric
summary: Aristotle's fourth-century BCE treatise defining rhetoric as the ability to see the available means of persuasion in a given case; it introduced the three proofs of character, emotion and argument, and the first systematic analysis of how an audience shapes a speech.

title: Audience analysis
summary: The practice of working out, before you write or speak, who will receive a message, what they already know, what they care about and what they need to do with it, and then shaping the content, structure, tone and channel to fit them.
selfCheck: Who will read or hear this - including people copied or forwarded to - and which of them is the one who must act?
What does my primary audience already know, and which of my terms or steps would they not recognise?
What is in this for them, and do they see it in the first few lines?
Have I checked my picture of the audience against something they actually said or did, or am I only guessing?
steps: List every audience, not just the addressee - the decision maker, technical reviewers, people who are copied, people the message may be forwarded to and people affected by the outcome.
For the primary audience, write down what they already know, what they care about, what attitude they are likely to bring and what they must decide or do after reading.
Check your assumptions against evidence - the questions people actually ask you, past replies, usage data or a short conversation with a typical reader.
Choose content, order, vocabulary, tone and channel to fit the primary audience, putting what matters to them first.
Give secondary audiences their own clearly labelled section instead of mixing material for different readers.
Reread the draft as each audience in turn - including someone it might be forwarded to - and fix what would confuse or alienate them.

example.situation: An engineering lead emails a delay notice about a data-platform migration to a list that includes the client's finance director.
example.before: Heads up - the ETL refactor slipped because the CDC connector kept OOMing on the backfill. New ETA is sprint 14, assuming infra gets us the bigger nodes.
example.after: Subject: Data migration finishing three weeks later than planned (no change to cost). The move to the new reporting system will finish on 4 December instead of 13 November. Your month-end reports will run on the old system as usual until then. Technical details for your IT team are in the section below.
example.why: The finance director is the primary reader and needs the date, the impact on her work and the cost; the jargon and team shorthand move to a separate section for the technical secondary audience.

title: BATNA
aliases: best alternative to a negotiated agreement
summary: Working out, before you negotiate, the best thing you will actually do if this negotiation fails - and using that alternative as the yardstick for every offer, the basis of your walk-away point and a source of leverage you can deliberately improve.
selfCheck: Do I know concretely what I will do tomorrow if this negotiation ends without a deal?
Have I compared my alternative with the offer on equivalent terms, or only on the headline price?
Is my opening ask set by my goal, or have I let a weak alternative drag it down?
Is everything I am about to say about my alternatives true?
steps: Before the first meeting, list every realistic thing you could do if no deal is reached - other vendors, other candidates, building it in-house, waiting, or doing nothing.
Translate each alternative into the same terms as the deal on the table (total cost, scope, risk, timing, effort to switch) so you are comparing like with like.
Pick the single best alternative - that is your BATNA - and from it set your reservation value, the worst deal you would still accept over walking away.
Spend some preparation time improving the BATNA itself (get a real competing quote, line up a second option) rather than only describing it.
Estimate the other side's BATNA too, and ask about their alternatives, so you know how much they need this deal.
Anchor your opening ask on your goal, not on your BATNA; keep a weak BATNA to yourself and never invent an alternative you do not have.
Re-check the BATNA whenever new information arrives during the talks, and walk away only when an offer is genuinely worse than it.

example.situation: An operations manager is renegotiating an annual software contract after the vendor proposes a 12% price rise.
example.before: We really can't move away from you, so please do what you can on the price. What's the best you can offer?
example.after: We've priced a comparable tool that would cost us about 8% less in year one, including migration. We'd rather stay - the team knows your product - so we're looking for a renewal at last year's rate with the new reporting module included. What would make that work on your side?
example.why: The manager did the BATNA homework first (a real, like-for-like competing quote), so the ask is anchored on a goal rather than on desperation, the alternative is mentioned truthfully without a threat, and the question invites the vendor to solve the problem with them.

title: Bottom line up front
summary: Opening a message with its conclusion, recommendation or request - the one thing the reader must know or do - and only then giving the background and supporting detail.
selfCheck: If my reader read only the subject line and first two sentences, would they know what I need from them and by when?
Have I stated my conclusion or recommendation, or only described the situation and left the reader to infer it?
Is this message an exception - serious bad news, or a reader who expects context first - and have I chosen the structure on purpose?
steps: Before drafting, write one sentence that states your conclusion, recommendation or request, including any decision and deadline you need.
Make that sentence (after a short purpose statement if the format calls for one) the opening of the message, and echo it in the subject line or title.
Add only the background the reader needs to act on it, most important first, and move history and method to the end or an attachment.
Put any secondary requests or audiences in clearly labelled sections below the main point.
Reread only the first two lines and ask whether a busy reader could act on them alone; if not, rewrite them.
Decide deliberately whether this message is an exception - serious bad news or a reader who expects context first - and if so use an indirect structure on purpose rather than by habit.

example.situation: A project analyst emails her director about a vendor problem that needs a decision.
example.before: Hi Sam, I wanted to give you some background on the reporting vendor. Over the last two months we have seen several late deliveries, and after a call with their account team on Tuesday it looks like their new platform will not support our quarterly export. I have looked at a few options...
example.after: Subject: Decision needed by Thursday - switch reporting vendor for Q1. Sam, I recommend we move the Q1 reports to our backup vendor; it adds about two weeks of setup but keeps the March board deadline. Please approve or decline by Thursday. Background: our current vendor's new platform cannot produce the quarterly export (confirmed on Tuesday's call), and deliveries have been late twice since September.
example.why: The recommendation, the decision asked for and the deadline appear in the subject line and first two sentences, so the director can act without reading the history, which is still there for anyone who wants it.

title: Channel selection
summary: Deliberately choosing the medium for a message - in person, video, phone, chat, email or a document - according to whether the job is to transmit information or to build shared understanding, how much tone and feedback matter, and what the receiver needs to do with it.
selfCheck: Am I mainly passing information on, or do we need to reach agreement - and does my channel fit that job?
If my reader misread the tone of this text, what is the worst plausible interpretation, and would a call prevent it?
Am I choosing email or chat because it suits the message, or because it lets me avoid an awkward conversation?
After a live discussion, have I put the decision, owners and dates in writing?
steps: Name the job of the message in one line - is it mainly to pass on information the receiver can absorb alone (conveyance), or to agree on meaning, resolve disagreement or decide something together (convergence)?
For conveyance - updates, data, instructions, reference material - default to a written, asynchronous channel the receiver can reread and process in their own time.

For convergence - an ambiguous problem, a disagreement, a sensitive or emotional message, or a request you need someone to say yes to - default to a live channel with voice and fast feedback, such as a call, video or a face-to-face conversation.

If tone, sarcasm or humour carries part of the meaning, either move to voice or rewrite the text so the meaning survives without your tone of voice; read it aloud in a deliberately flat or opposite tone before sending.
Combine channels when the task needs both - send the facts in writing first, discuss live, then confirm the decision and owners in writing.
Check the receiver's side - their familiarity with you and the topic, time zone, norms and access - and adjust the default; a lean channel works better between people who already share context.

example.situation: A project manager needs a client's sign-off to cut a feature so the release can stay on date, and the client sponsor is known to be attached to that feature.
example.before: Email, sent at 6 pm - Subject: Scope change. Hi Priya, given the integration issues we will need to drop the reporting module from the March release. Let me know if that works. Thanks.
example.after: Short email first - Subject: Decision needed Thursday - reporting module vs. March date. Priya, I'd like 20 minutes Wednesday to talk through a trade-off: keep the March date by moving the reporting module to April, or keep the module and slip to mid-April. One-page options summary attached. Then a 20-minute call to discuss, followed the same day by a written recap of the decision, owner and new dates.
example.why: The facts travel in writing where they can be reread, the contested decision happens live where questions and concerns surface immediately, and the written recap locks in the shared understanding the call produced.

title: Curse of knowledge
summary: The difficulty of imagining what it is like not to know something you know, which leads informed people to overestimate what their audience already understands and to communicate in shorthand, abstractions and skipped steps.
selfCheck: Which terms, acronyms or steps in this message did I learn on the job rather than expect my reader to know?
If my reader had only this message and none of my background, what would they do next?
Have I asked someone outside the work to restate my point in their own words, or am I only judging clarity myself?

title: Difficult conversation
summary: A conversation you are tempted to avoid because the topic threatens the relationship, the other person's or your own self-image, or strong feelings on either side - raising a performance problem, disagreeing with a decision, delivering bad news or repairing a falling-out. It goes best when approached as a shared attempt to learn what happened, not a contest over who is right.

title: Direct vs. indirect feedback
summary: The contrast between stating criticism plainly, often intensified with "upgraders" such as "totally", and softening it with "downgraders", understatement or omission so the listener infers the problem; norms differ across cultures, but research shows the gap shifts with setting, status and urgency rather than following nationality alone.
selfCheck: If I strip out the softeners or intensifiers, what is the core message I am sending - and would this listener decode it the same way?
Am I about to deliver criticism in front of people who do not need to hear it?
Have I checked what the person understood, rather than assuming my politeness or bluntness landed as intended?

title: Effective Writing for Army Leaders
summary: A 1986 U.S. Department of the Army pamphlet (DA Pam 600-67) that told leaders how to enforce the Army Writing Standard - writing understood in one rapid reading - by putting the "bottom line" first, using active voice and short sentences, and coaching writers with a quick-screen edit.

title: Email
summary: The asynchronous, text-based channel most organisations use for requests, updates, decisions and records; it suits messages the reader can absorb and act on alone, and works best when each message is scannable, answer-first and explicit about what is needed and by when.

title: George Loewenstein
summary: Carnegie Mellon behavioural economist and psychologist who, with Colin Camerer and Martin Weber, put the "curse of knowledge" on the research map in 1989 and later proposed the information-gap theory of curiosity; both ideas explain why experts misjudge audiences and how to hold attention.

title: High- and low-context cultures
summary: Edward T. Hall's contrast between communication in which most meaning sits in shared context, relationships and nonverbal cues (high-context) and communication in which meaning is carried mainly by explicit words (low-context); widely taught for intercultural work, but its country rankings have weak empirical support.

title: I-statements
summary: Raising a problem by describing the other person's specific behaviour, its concrete effect on you and how you feel about it, phrased from your own point of view ("I…") rather than as an accusation or verdict about them ("You always…").
selfCheck: Have I described a specific behaviour I could point to, or slipped in a label, a motive or an "always"?
Is my "I feel…" a real feeling, or a disguised accusation such as "I feel that you don't care"?
Have I said anything that shows I understand the other person's side of the situation?
After I speak, am I ready to listen to their reaction rather than repeat my point louder?
steps: Before speaking, name one specific, observable behaviour (what was said or done, and when) instead of a trait or a pattern word like "always" or "never".
Work out the concrete, tangible effect that behaviour has on you or your work - time lost, rework, a missed commitment.
Identify the feeling underneath, and check whether anger is masking something more precise such as worry or frustration.
Say it in the first person in roughly this order - behaviour, effect, feeling - and, if useful, a request for what you would like instead.
Add one sentence that shows you see the other person's side (their constraints, intentions or pressures) before or after your own view.
Stop and listen; expect some defensiveness, reflect back what you hear, and send a clearer second I-statement only if the first one was not understood.

example.situation: A project lead raises a recurring problem with a colleague who sends status updates late on the morning of the weekly client call.
example.before: You never get your updates in on time. You're making the whole team look unprepared in front of the client.
example.after: I know Mondays are packed for you with the support queue. When the status update reaches me after 9 a.m. on call days, I can't check the numbers before we present them, and I get anxious that we'll give the client something wrong. Could we agree on Friday afternoon as the cut-off?
example.why: The rewrite replaces a character verdict ("never", "you're making") with one observable behaviour, its concrete effect and the speaker's own feeling, acknowledges the colleague's constraint, and ends with a specific request - the combination the 2018 rating study found least likely to provoke defensiveness.

title: Illusion of transparency
summary: The tendency to overestimate how clearly other people can see our internal states - our nerves, feelings and intentions - and, by extension, how plainly our messages convey what we meant, so we under-signal and fail to check understanding.
selfCheck: Have I actually said the thing I am assuming they already picked up from my tone or face?
In this email, would a reader who could not hear my voice know whether I was joking, annoyed or serious?
Did I check what they understood, or did I take their nod as proof?
Before this presentation, am I treating my racing heart as something the audience can see?

title: Influence without authority
summary: Getting help from colleagues, other teams, bosses or clients you cannot direct by treating them as potential allies, learning what they care about and offering something they value in return - the reciprocity-based "influence model" of Allan R. Cohen and David L. Bradford.
selfCheck: Do I know what this person is measured on and worried about right now, or am I guessing?
What can I offer that they would value, and is it something I can genuinely deliver?
Have I separated what I must have from what would merely be nice?
Would I be comfortable if they saw exactly how I planned this request, or does it rely on spin?
steps: Treat the person whose help you need as a potential ally, even if past dealings were tense, and drop any story that they are simply difficult.
Write down exactly what you need from them, which parts are essential and which are nice to have, and check that the request serves the work rather than only your own ambitions.
Diagnose their world - how they are measured and rewarded, what their boss expects, what their workload and pressures are this quarter.

List the currencies they are likely to value (resources, information, help, recognition, visibility, a link to a larger purpose) and the ones you can actually offer, including cheap ones you control yourself.
Assess the relationship; if trust is low, repair it first, and adapt to how they prefer to work (data or story, email or a quick call).
Make a concrete, honest offer that trades something they value for what you need, then deliver on it and keep in touch afterwards so the relationship exists before you need it again.

example.situation: A product analyst needs an engineer on another team to add tracking events before a launch, but has no authority over the engineer's priorities.
example.before: Hi, I need these six tracking events added before Thursday's release. It's important for the launch, so please prioritise it. Thanks!
example.after: Hi - I know your team is measured on the release shipping cleanly, so I don't want to add risk. Of the six events, two are essential for the launch review (sign-up and first purchase); the rest can wait a sprint. I've written the event specs and test cases so it should be about an hour of work, and I'll credit your team in the launch metrics readout to the VP. Would Wednesday morning work, or is there a better slot?
example.why: The rewrite shows an understanding of the engineer's goals, cuts the ask to what is essential, lowers the cost by doing the preparatory work, and offers currencies the engineer may value (less effort, visibility with leadership) instead of borrowing urgency the analyst has no standing to impose.

title: Mehrabian's 7-38-55 rule
summary: The popular claim that only 7% of a message's meaning comes from words, 38% from tone of voice and 55% from facial expression and body language; it overgeneralises two narrow 1967 lab studies about inconsistent cues for liking, and Mehrabian himself says it does not apply to communication in general.

title: Message Equivocality, Media Selection, and Manager Performance
summary: A 1987 MIS Quarterly article by Richard Daft, Robert Lengel and Linda Klebe Trevino that turned media richness theory into a claim about managerial skill: managers tend to send ambiguous messages through rich media and clear ones through lean media, and higher performers match the two more closely.

title: Open-ended questions
summary: Questions that cannot be answered with "yes", "no" or a single fact - typically starting with "what" or "how" - asked to let the other person explain in their own words, so you learn what they know, think and need rather than what you assumed.
selfCheck: Could the other person have answered my question with one word, and was that what I really wanted?
Did my next question build on their answer, or did I jump to my own agenda?
Did I ask a "why" question where a "what" or "how" would have felt less like a demand for justification?
When I needed a firm answer on a specific risk, did I ask a direct, specific question instead of a vague one?
steps: Decide what you actually need to learn - their view, the obstacles, the options - before you ask anything.
Open with "what" or "how" ("What's getting in the way?", "How did the client react?") instead of "Is", "Do" or "Did".
Stop talking and let them answer fully; resist offering a suggested answer if they pause.
Build your next question on what they just said ("You mentioned the handover - what happened there?") rather than switching topic.
Reflect back what you heard before asking another question, so the exchange does not become an interrogation.
Switch to a closed or specific question when you need a commitment, a number, or a straight answer to a known risk ("Will this slip past the 30th?").

example.situation: A team lead checks in with an engineer on a database migration that has gone quiet for a week.
example.before: Is the migration still on track for the end of the month?
example.after: What's the part of the migration you're least confident about right now?
example.why: The closed question invites a reflexive "yes"; the open one asks for an explanation and presumes there is some uncertainty, which makes it easier to surface a problem early.

title: Paraphrasing
summary: Restating, in your own words, the substance of what someone has just said - and, where it matters, the feeling and priority behind it - then checking whether you have understood them correctly before you respond with your own view.
selfCheck: Did I restate their point in my own words, or did I just repeat their phrases back like a parrot?
Did I capture what mattered to them and how they felt, not only the facts?
Did I end with a genuine check ("Have I got that right?") and accept a correction without defending myself?
Did I hold back my own view until they agreed I had understood them?
steps: Listen to the whole point without planning your reply; note the facts, what the speaker seems to feel and what seems most important to them.
Wait for a natural pause, then restate the core of their message in one or two sentences, using your own words rather than echoing theirs.
Where feelings are clearly present, name the feeling and its cause tentatively ("it sounds like the late change left you frustrated").
End with a check question such as "Have I got that right?" or "What did I miss?" and accept corrections without arguing.
If they correct you, paraphrase the corrected version; follow up with an open question if something is still unclear.
Only once they confirm you have understood, give your own perspective, answer or proposal.

example.situation: An operations lead tells a project manager that the new vendor's delivery schedule will not work for the warehouse, and the PM's instinct is to defend the schedule.
example.before: The schedule was signed off by procurement last month, so we really can't change it now. Let's just make it work.
example.after: So if I've understood you, the Tuesday deliveries land on the same morning as the weekly stock count, which means your team either delays the count or leaves trucks waiting - and you're worried we'll start paying demurrage. Is that the main problem, or is there more to it?
example.why: The rewrite restates the specific facts and the concern behind them in the PM's own words and invites correction, so the operations lead can confirm or fix the picture before anyone argues for a solution.

title: Plain language
summary: The principle of writing so that the intended readers can find what they need, understand it and use it the first time they read it, by writing for that audience in familiar words, clear structure and direct sentences.
selfCheck: Who exactly is reading this, and what do they already know about the subject?
Which terms here did I learn inside my team or field, and have I replaced or defined each one where it first appears?
Could a reader say in their own words what I want them to do next?

title: Psychological safety
summary: A shared belief among members of a team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks - to ask a question, admit a mistake, raise a concern or disagree - without being embarrassed, rejected or punished for it.

title: Situation-Behavior-Impact
summary: A three-part way to give feedback developed at the Center for Creative Leadership: name the specific situation, describe the observable behaviour, and say what impact it had on you - optionally followed by asking about the person's intent.
selfCheck: Could the other person picture the exact moment I mean, or did I say something vague like "lately"?
Is my behaviour description something a camera could record, or did I slip in a judgement or guess at a motive?
Have I said what the impact actually was, rather than assuming they already know?
Did I leave room to ask about their intent and listen before deciding what should change?
steps: Pin down the situation - the specific meeting, document or moment, with a time and place ("in Tuesday's 10 a.m. client call"), not "lately" or "last week".
Describe the behaviour as something a camera could have recorded - words said, actions taken - and strip out labels such as "rude", "lazy" or "great attitude".
State the impact the behaviour had on you, the team or the work, in your own voice, naming a concrete consequence and, if useful, your reaction (frustrated, relieved, proud).
For redirecting feedback, stop and ask about intent ("What were you aiming for there?") and listen before proposing any fix.
Agree together on what to keep doing or what to try next time, and give the feedback close to the event while it is still fresh.
Use the same three parts for positive feedback, so the person knows exactly which behaviour to repeat.

example.situation: A team lead gives feedback to an analyst who presented the quarterly numbers at a leadership review.
example.before: You came across as really unprepared today and kind of defensive. You need to step up your game before the next one.
example.after: In this morning's quarterly review with the VPs, when Priya asked where the churn figure came from, you said 'I'd have to check' and moved on. The VPs then questioned two other numbers and we lost ten minutes of the agenda, and I was worried they'd discount the whole forecast. What was going on for you at that point?
example.why: The rewrite swaps verdicts ("unprepared", "defensive") for a time-stamped situation, an observable behaviour and a concrete impact, then asks about intent - so the analyst can see exactly what to change and has room to explain instead of defending their character.

title: Teach-back
summary: Checking whether an explanation landed by asking the other person to explain it back, or show it, in their own words - framed as a test of how clearly you explained rather than of what they know - and re-explaining until their version is right.
selfCheck: Did I ask them to say it in their own words, or did I accept a nod or a "makes sense"?
Did I frame the check as testing my explanation, not their competence?
Which one or two points would cause real damage if misunderstood, and did I check those?
When their restatement was off, did I re-explain differently rather than repeat myself louder?
steps: Pick the one to three points the other person must get right to act - a deadline, a decision, a sequence of steps - rather than checking everything.
Explain each point in plain, specific language, one point at a time.
Take ownership of the check out loud, for example "I want to make sure I explained that clearly."
Ask an open request to restate or demonstrate ("How will you walk the client through this?"), never a yes/no question such as "Does that make sense?"
Listen for gaps or errors; if you hear one, re-explain that part differently and ask again until their version is accurate.
Close by confirming the agreed version in writing where it matters (a recap message or ticket).

example.situation: A team lead hands over an urgent client escalation to a colleague before going on leave.
example.before: So that's the background - escalate to Priya's team if the patch fails, and keep the client posted. Does that all make sense?
example.after: I've thrown a lot at you, so let me check I explained it well. If the patch fails on Thursday, what are your next two moves, and who hears from you first?
example.why: The yes/no check invites a polite "yes"; the open request surfaces the missing piece (who to call first) while the lead can still fix it, and frames any gap as the explainer's problem.

title: William Strunk Jr.
summary: Cornell English professor (1869-1946) whose 1918 classroom handbook, The Elements of Style, set out short imperative rules such as using the active voice and omitting needless words; revised by his former student E. B. White in 1959, it became the best-known American writing guide.

title: Words of estimative probability
summary: Stating how likely something is with an agreed set of likelihood words, each tied to a numeric range that is shown next to the word, so that "likely" means the same thing to the writer and every reader.
selfCheck: If three readers each wrote down the percentage they think my likelihood word means, would their numbers land in the same range as mine?
Have I put the number next to the word, or am I relying on readers to look up a key they will probably skip?
Am I using "could", "may" or "possible" to hedge when I actually have an estimate I am reluctant to commit to?
Have I kept my confidence in the evidence separate from the likelihood of the event?
steps: Agree a short likelihood scale with your team or client before you need it - for example remote (under 5%), unlikely (20-45%), roughly even (45-55%), likely (55-80%), very likely (80-95%) - with ranges that do not overlap.
Before writing a forecast, decide your own number or range first, then pick the one word on the scale whose range contains it.
Put the numeric range in brackets right after the word in the text itself ("likely (55-80%)"), not in a footnote, appendix or hover text.
Keep likelihood (how probable the event is) separate from confidence (how solid your evidence is), and say each in its own sentence.
Reserve "possible", "could" and "may" for cases where you genuinely cannot estimate the odds, and say so rather than using them as softeners.
Use the same words with the same meanings in every report, and add a short key whenever a new reader joins the distribution.

example.situation: A consultant updates a client steering committee on whether a system migration will hit its go-live date.
example.before: There is a real possibility we could miss the March 1 go-live, although the team is working hard and it may well still be achievable.
example.after: We judge it unlikely (20-45%) that we hit the March 1 go-live; very likely (80-95%) by March 22. We have moderate confidence: the estimate rests on two weeks of test-defect data. Decision needed by Friday: hold the date with reduced scope, or move it.
example.why: The before version could be read anywhere from a small risk to a probable slip; the after version gives one shared range, separates odds from confidence, and turns the forecast into a decision the committee can make.
